17630: A yardstick is something used to measure or judge how good, how successful, or how correct something is. Think of it as your personal ruler for making comparisons.

This word carries two meanings: one literal and one figurative. Both are important to know.

Meaning 1 — The Physical Object (Literal)

A yardstick, in its most direct sense, is a flat, straight measuring stick that is exactly one yard long (which equals 36 inches, or about 91 centimetres). It looks like a long, thin ruler. Carpenters, tailors, and craftspeople use it to measure wood, fabric, or any surface with precision.

"She used a yardstick to measure the length of the curtain fabric."

This is the original, straightforward meaning.

Meaning 2 — A Standard for Judgement (Figurative) ⬅ The More Important One

This is where the word truly comes alive, and it is by far the more common way this word is used — in everyday conversation, in newspapers, in business, and in literature.

When used figuratively, a yardstick means a fixed standard, benchmark, or criterion that you use to evaluate, compare, or judge something or someone.

Just like a physical yardstick gives you an exact, unchanging length to measure things against, a figurative yardstick gives you a reliable point of reference to judge whether something is good or bad, successful or unsuccessful, fair or unfair.

Think of it this way:

Imagine you are hiring a chef. You decide that the yardstick for choosing the best chef is how perfectly they can cook a three-course meal in under an hour. Every applicant is judged against that one fixed standard — your yardstick. Anyone who meets it passes. Anyone who doesn't, fails.

The yardstick here is not a physical stick. It is an idea, a rule, or a measure of quality that you use to judge everything else.

• "Profit is not the only yardstick of a company's success."

Here, "yardstick" means the standard being used to decide if a company is doing well. The speaker is saying profit shouldn't be the only measure — other things, like employee happiness or environmental impact, should also matter.

  • "His first novel became the yardstick against which all his later work was measured."

His debut novel set such a high standard that every book he wrote after it was compared to that one to see if it was better, worse, or equal.

  • "Test scores are an imperfect yardstick for measuring a student's intelligence."

Exam results are being used as a measuring standard for intelligence, but the speaker feels this standard is flawed.

For something to be called a yardstick (in the figurative sense), it must do three things:

  1. It must be a standard — a clear, specific point of reference, not something vague.
  2. It must be used for comparison — you measure something else against it.
  3. It must help you make a judgement — it tells you whether something is adequate, superior, or falling short.

These words are close in meaning and can often be used in place of "yardstick":

  • Benchmark — a reference point used to measure performance. Very common in business and technology. (e.g., "The new phone set a benchmark for battery life.")
  • Standard — a level of quality or requirement that is accepted as normal or desirable.
  • Criterion (plural: criteria) — a specific rule or principle by which something is judged. (e.g., "Price is one criterion; quality is another.")
  • Measure — a way of assessing something.
  • Barometer — similar to yardstick but often used when something indicates a broader condition, like a mood or a trend. (e.g., "Box office earnings are a barometer of public taste.")

The subtle difference with yardstick specifically is that it carries a strong sense of a single, definite standard used to judge or compare — like one clear ruler that everyone agrees to measure against.

A yardstick is neutral by nature — it is simply a tool for judgement. But the word is often used in contexts where someone is either:

  • Praising a standard as fair and reliable:

"Customer satisfaction should be the yardstick for every business decision."

  • Criticising a standard as too narrow, unfair, or misleading:

"Using salary alone as the yardstick for a person's worth is deeply misguided."

So pay attention to the surrounding words in a sentence — they'll tell you whether the speaker thinks the yardstick being used is a good or bad one.

A yardstick is a fixed standard used to judge or compare how good, successful, or valid something is — like a ruler, but for ideas, performance, or quality.

Whenever you see or hear this word, ask yourself: "What is being measured, and what is the thing it's being compared against?" Answer those two questions, and the sentence will always make perfect sense.
17631: A yarmulke is a small, round cap — roughly the size of your palm — that Jewish men wear on top of their head. It sits on the crown of the head (the upper-back part), not pulled down over the ears like a regular hat. It covers only a small portion of the head.

It is a soft, brimless cap. It can be made from many materials — velvet, suede, leather, or knitted wool/cotton. It comes in many colors and patterns, though plain black or white ones are common. Some are very small and subtle; others are larger and more visible. The style a person chooses often signals something about their background or level of religious observance.

Jewish men wear it. How often depends on the individual and their Jewish community:

  • Strictly observant (Orthodox) Jewish men wear it every waking hour, all day long, every day of their lives. For them, removing it is unusual.
  • Less strictly observant Jewish men may wear it only during prayer, religious study, or while inside a synagogue (a Jewish house of worship).
  • Some Jewish men choose not to wear it at all — this is considered acceptable in more liberal branches of Judaism.

In some more progressive Jewish communities, women also wear yarmulkes, though this is not traditional.

The yarmulke is worn as an act of respect and humility before God. The idea behind it is that wearing something on your head is a constant, physical reminder that God is above you — above all human beings. It is a way of acknowledging a higher presence at all times.

It is not commanded directly in the written Torah (the Jewish scripture), but it became a deeply rooted tradition over centuries, especially in observant communities, where it eventually took on the weight of religious obligation.

The word yarmulke comes from Yiddish (the language historically spoken by Jews in Eastern Europe). The same item is also called a kippah — this is the Hebrew word for it, and kippah simply means "dome" or "covering." Both words refer to the exact same object. In Israel and in Hebrew-speaking contexts, you'll hear kippah more often. In everyday English conversation, both words are used and understood.
As a symbol of Jewish identity

Beyond its religious meaning, the yarmulke has become one of the most visible and widely recognized symbols of Jewish identity in the world. When someone wears one in public, it is often a conscious, open declaration: I am Jewish, and I am not hiding it.

Because of this, the choice of whether to wear a yarmulke in public can carry personal weight — some Jews see it as an act of pride and courage, especially in parts of the world where being visibly Jewish has historically brought risk.

When a non-Jewish person visits a synagogue, attends a Jewish religious ceremony (like a bar mitzvah or bat mitzvah — a coming-of-age celebration), or visits certain holy Jewish sites, they are often given a yarmulke to wear as a sign of respect for the space and the occasion. This is considered a polite, welcoming gesture, not a religious conversion of any kind. You simply put it on, participate respectfully, and return it when you leave.

A yarmulke is a small head cap worn by Jewish men (and sometimes women) as an expression of humility before God and as a marker of Jewish religious identity. It is one of the most recognizable symbols of Judaism, carrying both deep spiritual meaning and strong cultural significance.
17632: The word yarn has two separate meanings as a noun — one concrete and physical, the other informal and figurative. Both are important and widely used in English.
Meaning 1 — A Material: Twisted Strands of Fiber

Yarn is a long, continuous, thread-like strand made by twisting together many short, loose fibers. It is the fundamental raw material used to make fabric, clothing, blankets, scarves, and many other textiles.

Picture the soft, fluffy material wound into a ball that you would find in a craft store or in a grandmother's knitting basket. That is yarn.

What is yarn made from?

Yarn can come from natural sources or from synthetic (man-made) materials. Natural yarns include wool (from sheep), cotton (from the cotton plant), silk (from silkworms), cashmere (from goats), linen, and alpaca. Synthetic yarns include acrylic, polyester, nylon, and rayon. Different materials give different qualities — wool is warm and stretchy, cotton is cool and breathable, and acrylic is affordable and easy to wash.

How is yarn made?

Short, loose fibers are spun — that is, twisted — together to form a single continuous strand. Multiple strands can then be twisted together again to make the yarn thicker and more durable. This process of combining strands is called plying. When you see a yarn labeled "2-ply," it simply means two strands have been twisted together into one.

What is yarn used for?

Yarn is the starting material for knitting (using two long needles to loop yarn into fabric), crocheting (using a hook to form interlocked loops), weaving (threading yarn through a loom to create cloth), and various forms of needlework and embroidery.

How is yarn different from thread and string?

These three words confuse many learners, so here is a precise comparison:

Thread is much, much thinner than yarn. It is used in sewing machines or for hand-stitching to join pieces of fabric together. Think of the thin line you pass through a needle's eye to stitch a button back onto a shirt.

String is typically thicker and rougher than yarn, usually made from twisted plant fibers or synthetic material, and is used for tying or binding things — not for making cloth. Think of the string tied around a parcel.

Yarn is softer than string, thicker than thread, and its purpose is specifically for textile crafts such as knitting, weaving, and crocheting.

A useful way to picture the size order: thread → yarn → string → rope. Each one gets progressively thicker and rougher.

Thickness of yarn

Yarn comes in a range of thicknesses, which crafters refer to as "weight." The thinnest yarns (called lace or fingering weight) produce fine, delicate fabric. Medium yarns (called DK or worsted weight) are the most commonly used for everyday projects. The thickest yarns (called bulky or super bulky) create heavy, warm fabric very quickly. As a general rule: the thicker the yarn, the faster a project is completed, and the warmer the finished piece tends to be.
Meaning 2 — A Story: An Informal, Often Exaggerated Tale

In informal English, yarn also means a long, entertaining story — particularly one that is adventurous, colorful, or exciting in nature.

What makes a yarn different from just any story is its particular character. It is the kind of tale told in a relaxed, convivial setting — around a campfire, in a pub, on a ship's deck — where the storyteller brings it to life with great enthusiasm and dramatic flair. Crucially, a yarn is often exaggerated or embellished. The storyteller is likely stretching the truth somewhat to make the tale more gripping and entertaining. The listener usually knows this and enjoys it anyway.

Example: "The old sailor sat down and spun us a yarn about the enormous shark he once wrestled off the coast of Portugal."

The phrase spin a yarn is one of the most common idioms in English, and it means to tell one of these long, lively, embellished stories. If someone says, "He was spinning a yarn," they mean he was weaving an elaborate tale — and the implication is that the listener might be wise to take parts of it with a pinch of salt.

This second meaning of yarn is informal in register and is most commonly heard in British, Australian, and Irish English, though it is understood throughout the English-speaking world.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Context makes this effortless:

If someone is talking about knitting, crocheting, a craft store, fabric, fibers, or textiles — they mean the physical material: long twisted strands of fiber.

If someone is talking about storytelling, a traveler's tale, an old sailor, a campfire, or something that might be exaggerated — they mean a long, entertaining, and possibly embellished story.

The two meanings never overlap in practice, so there is virtually no risk of confusion once you know both.
17633: A yashmak is a type of face veil traditionally worn by some Muslim women, most closely associated with Ottoman Turkey and certain parts of the broader Islamic world.

A yashmak is not a single piece of cloth. It is made up of two separate pieces of thin fabric — usually white or a light color — worn together on the face:

  • One piece covers the upper part of the face: from the forehead down to just above or at the bridge of the nose.
  • The other piece covers the lower part of the face: from just below the eyes, covering the nose, mouth, and chin.

When both pieces are in place, they overlap slightly in the middle, and the result is that only the eyes are left uncovered. Everything else — forehead, nose, cheeks, mouth, chin — is hidden behind the fabric.

The yashmak is rooted in the Islamic tradition of modesty (known more broadly as purdah or hijab — the general principle of modest covering for women in public). In cultures where this tradition was practiced strictly, women would cover not just their hair and body, but also their face when going out. The yashmak was the specific garment used to fulfill that face-covering requirement.

It was especially common during the Ottoman Empire era, where it was a standard part of a respectable woman's appearance in public.
How it differs from similar veils

This is important, because there are several kinds of face and head coverings in Islamic tradition, and they are not the same thing:

  • Hijab — covers the hair, ears, and neck, but leaves the face fully visible. Very widely worn today.
  • Niqab — a face veil that covers everything except the eyes, usually made of a single piece of fabric. Similar in effect to the yashmak, but typically one piece, not two.
  • Burqa — covers the entire body from head to toe, including the face, but with a mesh screen over the eye area so the woman can see out while remaining entirely hidden.
  • Yashmak — specifically a two-piece arrangement covering the face, leaving only the eyes exposed. Its defining feature is this double-cloth construction.

So the yashmak sits somewhere close to the niqab in terms of how much it covers, but it is a distinct garment with its own traditional form.
What it looks like in practice

Imagine a woman standing in a busy marketplace. She is wearing a long robe and a headscarf. But when you look at her face, you see only her eyes — the rest of her face is covered by two layers of thin, pale fabric that meet across the bridge of the nose. That is the yashmak. The fabric is usually fine and lightweight, not thick or heavy, so it is not suffocating to wear.

The yashmak, in its traditional Ottoman form, is largely historical today. It was most common in the 19th and early 20th centuries and declined as the Ottoman Empire gave way to modern Turkey, which moved toward more Westernized dress codes. However, the broader idea of face-covering veils continues in various forms (like the niqab) across different parts of the Muslim world.

You might encounter the word "yashmak" today primarily in:

  • Historical writing about the Ottoman period
  • Literature from the 19th or early 20th century
  • Dictionary or vocabulary contexts (as a relatively rare English word for a specific cultural garment)

A yashmak is a traditional veil made of two pieces of thin fabric, worn by some Muslim women to cover the face in public, leaving only the eyes visible — most historically associated with Ottoman Turkey.
17634:
Yaw is a specific type of rotational movement. It describes the side-to-side swinging of a moving object — its front (nose, bow, or tip) turning left or right around an imaginary vertical axis, like a spinning top rotating flat on a table.

The easiest way to picture it: stand still and shake your head "no." Your head rotates left, then right, around a vertical line running down your spine. That motion — horizontal rotation around a vertical axis — is exactly what yaw is.
The three rotations every vehicle can make

To understand yaw properly, you need to know that any vehicle in motion — an airplane, a ship, a rocket, a car — can rotate in three distinct ways. Each has its own name:

Pitch — the front tilts up or down. Think of nodding your head "yes," or a plane climbing or diving.

Roll — the vehicle tilts sideways along its length. Think of tilting your head toward your shoulder, or a plane banking to one side.

Yaw — the front swings left or right while the vehicle stays level. This is our word.

These three — pitch, roll, and yaw — are the complete vocabulary for describing how a vehicle is oriented in space. Yaw is always the horizontal, flat-spin rotation around the vertical axis.
What "yaw" refers to as a noun

As a noun, yaw can mean two related things:

  1. An instance of this side-to-side rotation — "The ship experienced a sudden yaw to port." This means the bow (front) of the ship swung to the left.
  2. The angle of that rotation — "A yaw of 15 degrees." This means the vehicle's nose has rotated 15 degrees away from the direction it was originally pointing.
Where you will meet this word

Aviation — In a plane, yaw is controlled by the rudder (the vertical fin at the tail). When the rudder deflects one way, the tail is pushed the opposite way, and the nose swings sideways. Pilots manage yaw carefully, especially during takeoff and landing. There is a well-known phenomenon called adverse yaw — when a pilot rolls the plane to one side, the nose involuntarily yaws in the opposite direction as a side effect. Correcting this is part of basic flying technique.

Ships and sailing — A ship yaws when waves, currents, or wind push its bow off the intended course. Holding a straight heading in rough seas requires constant correction against yaw. You might read: "Heavy swells caused the vessel to yaw unpredictably."

Spacecraft and missiles — Rockets and missiles must be carefully controlled in all three axes. A yaw during a rocket launch means the nose is pointing off the intended trajectory. Mission controllers track yaw in real time. A yaw maneuver is when a spacecraft intentionally rotates around its vertical axis — for example, to point an antenna toward Earth or align with a docking port.

Automotive engineering — Cars also yaw. When you turn a steering wheel, the car rotates around its vertical axis — that is yaw. Yaw rate is the technical term for how quickly this rotation is happening (measured in degrees per second). Too much yaw at high speed means the car is spinning out. Electronic stability control systems in modern cars work by measuring yaw rate and applying brakes to individual wheels to bring the car back under control.

Wind turbines — A wind turbine must always face directly into the wind to work efficiently. The mechanism that rotates the entire top of the turbine (the nacelle and blades) to track the wind is called the yaw system. When the turbine is not properly aligned with the wind, that misalignment is called yaw error.

Ballistics — A bullet is spin-stabilized (the rifling of a gun barrel makes it rotate rapidly along its flight axis, like a football spiral). A well-fired bullet has near-zero yaw — its nose points almost exactly in the direction of travel. But if the bullet is destabilized — by wind, imperfect firing, or impact with an object — its nose begins to swing off-axis. This is the bullet's yaw. Greater yaw means greater air resistance (drag) and less accuracy.
Key compound terms you will encounter

Yaw axis — the imaginary vertical line through the center of a vehicle, around which yaw rotation occurs.

Yaw rate — how fast the yaw rotation is happening, usually measured in degrees per second.

Yaw angle — the number of degrees a vehicle has rotated horizontally away from a reference direction (its original heading, or a target direction).

Yaw control — the systems responsible for managing and correcting yaw.

Yaw stability — a vehicle's natural tendency to resist unwanted yaw and return to its original heading. A vehicle with good yaw stability does not easily get pushed off course.

Adverse yaw — an unwanted yaw caused as a side effect of another maneuver (most commonly rolling an aircraft).
An important distinction: yaw is rotation, not travel

Yaw describes which way the vehicle is pointing, not necessarily which way it is moving. A ship can yaw 10 degrees to the right — meaning its bow rotates rightward — while still being carried forward (or even sideways) by momentum and currents. Similarly, a bullet can yaw (its nose tips sideways) while its overall path through the air barely changes. The rotation and the trajectory are separate things, even though uncontrolled yaw usually leads to a change in trajectory over time.

Yaw (noun) is the rotational movement of a vehicle or object around its vertical axis — the front (nose, bow, or tip) swings left or right while the vehicle remains otherwise level. It is one of the three fundamental axes of rotation (alongside pitch and roll) used in aviation, navigation, spacecraft engineering, automotive dynamics, and ballistics. As a noun, it names the specific type of motion itself, an instance of it occurring, or the angle by which the rotation has happened.
17635:
To yaw means to rotate or swing around a vertical axis — that is, to swivel left or right from a fixed heading, like a compass needle spinning on its pivot. The key thing to understand is that yawing is purely a rotational side-to-side movement. The object doesn't tilt up or down, and it doesn't roll sideways — it simply spins horizontally around an imaginary vertical pole running through it from top to bottom.

Think of yourself standing still and turning your head left and right. Your head is yawing. Your body doesn't lean; your chin doesn't dip — the movement is purely horizontal rotation.
Why "Yaw" Exists as Its Own Word

To truly understand yaw, you need to know that any vehicle moving through space (a plane, a ship, a rocket) can rotate in exactly three independent ways. Each has its own name:

1. Roll — Rotation around the front-to-back axis.
Imagine a plane spinning like a drill bit as it flies forward. Or a log rolling down a hill. That's roll.

2. Pitch — Rotation around the side-to-side axis.
A plane's nose tilts upward to climb, or downward to dive. A ship's bow rises over a wave and crashes down. That's pitch.

3. Yaw — Rotation around the top-to-bottom axis.
The nose of a plane or the bow of a ship swings left or right while everything else stays level. That is yaw.

These three are completely distinct. You can roll without pitching or yawing. You can yaw without rolling or pitching. Engineers, pilots, and sailors need separate words for each because each is controlled by different mechanisms and has different effects. Yaw is the one that handles directional deviation — swinging off to one side.

When a pilot says a plane is yawing, it means the nose is swinging sideways — left or right — while the wings remain level. This is controlled by the rudder, a movable fin on the tail that pushes the tail left or right, which in turn points the nose the opposite way.

Yaw in flight can be:

  • Intentional — a pilot deliberately applies rudder input to align the nose with the runway during a crosswind landing, or to coordinate a turn.
  • Unintional — a gust of wind, engine failure (on a multi-engine aircraft), or aerodynamic forces can cause the plane to yaw unexpectedly, which the pilot must correct.

A specific and important example: when a plane banks into a turn, the outer wing naturally generates slightly more lift and drag than the inner wing. This asymmetry tends to swing the nose in the wrong direction — a phenomenon called adverse yaw — which pilots counteract with rudder input.

A ship yaws when its bow (front) swings off its intended course to one side or the other. Unlike in aviation, yawing at sea is often caused by external forces:

  • Following seas (waves hitting from behind) can push the stern sideways, causing the bow to swing.
  • Strong crosswinds can push the hull and superstructure, rotating the ship off course.
  • Currents hitting the hull unevenly can cause the bow to swing.

A helmsman's job is partly to counteract yaw — to constantly make small corrections to keep the ship on its intended heading. If a ship yaws excessively and the helmsman overcorrects, it can begin a back-and-forth swinging called yawing motion, which is uncomfortable, slows the vessel, and wastes fuel.

In space, all three axes of rotation matter enormously because there is no atmosphere to stabilize a craft. A spacecraft yaws when its nose swings left or right relative to its direction of travel. Mission controllers and onboard computers constantly make tiny yaw adjustments to keep the vehicle pointed correctly — whether that means keeping a rocket aligned during ascent, pointing a satellite's antenna toward Earth, or orienting a space telescope toward a target.
Yaw in Everyday and Informal Use

Outside of technical contexts, the verb "yaw" can be used more loosely to describe any vehicle or object suddenly veering or swinging off to one side:

  • A car fishtailing on ice is yawing.
  • A shopping trolley with a bad wheel that keeps swinging sideways is yawing.
  • A bullet or arrow that begins to rotate off its axis in flight is yawing (which kills accuracy).

In these everyday uses, the word simply captures the idea of an unintended or sudden sideways deviation or swing.

• The small aircraft began to yaw sharply to the left when the crosswind picked up.
  • Without constant rudder corrections, the ship would yaw off its course within minutes.
  • The rocket yawed slightly during launch, but the guidance system corrected it instantly.
  • Ice on the road caused the truck to yaw violently before the driver regained control.
  • The bullet began to yaw in flight after striking the first obstacle, losing all accuracy.

To yaw is to rotate around a vertical axis — for a vehicle, this means its nose or front end swings sideways (left or right) relative to its direction of travel, whether intentionally or as a result of external forces.
17636: A yawl is a type of sailboat — specifically, a boat with two masts (the tall vertical poles that hold the sails).

Most small sailboats have just one mast. A yawl has two. What makes a yawl special — and different from other two-masted boats — is where the second mast sits and how big it is.

Here's how it works:

  • The first mast (called the mainmast) is the tall one. It sits roughly toward the middle-front of the boat and carries the largest sails.
  • The second mast (called the mizzenmast, or sometimes the "jigger") is much shorter and thinner. It sits all the way at the very back of the boat — so far back that it's actually behind the rudder post (the rudder post is the pivot point that the steering mechanism — the rudder — rotates around).

That last detail is the key. The mizzenmast being placed behind the rudder post is what officially defines a yawl. This tiny back mast is often quite small, almost like an afterthought compared to the main mast.
Why does a yawl have this second mast?

The small mizzenmast and its sail aren't there to drive the boat forward powerfully. Instead, they act more like a balancing tool. Sailors use it to help steer and stabilize the boat — especially in heavy wind or rough conditions. Think of it like a small fin at the back of a paper airplane that keeps it flying straight.

Because of this, a yawl is considered a very practical and manageable boat. A single sailor can handle one without too much difficulty, even in challenging weather, because the sail plan is well-balanced and flexible.
How a yawl compares to its close cousin: the ketch

The yawl is very often confused with another two-masted sailboat called a ketch. They look almost identical from a distance. The one and only real structural difference is this:

  • On a ketch, the second mast is placed in front of the rudder post — meaning it's slightly closer to the center of the boat.
  • On a yawl, the second mast is placed behind the rudder post — meaning it's pushed further toward the very stern (back end) of the boat.

Because the mizzenmast on a ketch sits in a more central position, it can carry a bigger sail and contribute more to actually moving the boat. The mizzenmast on a yawl, being pushed so far back, is smaller and contributes less to propulsion — its job is mostly balance and steering control.

A simple way to remember: if the back mast looks almost like it's hanging off the very tail of the boat, barely fitting before the water begins, it's likely a yawl.

In older, more historical usage — and still in some nautical contexts today — "yawl" also refers to a small utility boat (also called a ship's boat or tender) that used to be carried on board large sailing ships.

This was a small, sturdy open boat, typically rowed by several oarsmen, sometimes with a small sail. Large ships couldn't always dock directly at a port or shore, so they would lower this small yawl into the water to ferry passengers, crew, and supplies back and forth. Think of it as the "taxi" that a big ship kept on deck for short trips.

This meaning is much less common today, since modern ships don't use rowboats as tenders in the same way. When you encounter "yawl" in contemporary sailing writing or conversation, it almost always refers to the two-masted sailboat described above.

A yawl is a two-masted sailboat whose defining feature is a small second mast placed at the very back of the boat, behind the rudder post. This second mast carries a small sail used mainly for balance and steering, not speed. Yawls are known for being manageable and well-balanced, making them a practical choice for sailing. The word also has an older meaning referring to a small rowing/sailing utility boat carried aboard large ships.
17637:
To yawn means to open your mouth very wide, breathe in a long, deep breath of air, and then breathe it back out — usually slowly. It often comes with a sound, like a soft moan or sigh, and sometimes your eyes water a little when you do it. Your jaw stretches as far as it can go, and the whole thing lasts just a few seconds before your mouth closes again.

This is something your body does mostly on its own — you don't really decide to do it. It just happens.

There are a few common situations that trigger a yawn:

When you are tired or sleepy. This is the most familiar one. When your body needs rest and your brain is slowing down, you yawn. Think of the feeling of lying in bed early in the morning, slowly waking up — you almost certainly yawn in those moments.

When you are bored. If something is dull, unstimulating, or going on for too long, your body can respond with a yawn. This is why yawning is often associated with disinterest. Saying someone "yawned through the whole lecture" paints a clear picture of someone who found it completely uninteresting.

When you are waking up or about to fall asleep. Yawning happens a lot at the edges of sleep — right when you're transitioning between being awake and being asleep.

Sometimes when you are anxious or nervous. Less obviously, some people yawn when they feel stressed or anxious, because the body is trying to take in more oxygen and regulate itself.
The Involuntary Nature — An Important Detail

One of the most important things to understand about yawning is that it is largely involuntary — meaning you don't usually choose to do it, it just happens to you. You can try to yawn on purpose, and sometimes you can, but most real yawns simply arrive on their own. You can also suppress a yawn (hold it back, keep your mouth shut), but that takes effort, and the urge is often strong.

This involuntary quality is why yawning in public — especially in a meeting, a class, or during a conversation — is considered impolite in many cultures. It can look like you're bored or uninterested, even if you're not. Politely covering your mouth with your hand while yawning is the social norm in most places.

Here is a fascinating truth about this word: yawning is famously contagious. When you see someone else yawn, or even just read or think about yawning, you may feel the urge to yawn yourself. This is a well-known and widely experienced phenomenon. Even reading this explanation right now may be making you want to yawn — and that is completely normal.

Beyond the physical act that humans and animals do, yawn is also used figuratively to describe something that opens up in a wide, gaping way — like a large hole, a deep gap, or an empty space stretching before you.

For example:

  • "A deep chasm yawned at their feet." — Here, the chasm (a large crack in the earth) isn't literally yawning of course, but the image works perfectly: the gap opens wide and deep, just like a mouth does when yawning.
  • "A vast emptiness yawned before her." — This conveys that a huge, open, intimidating space stretched out in front of her.

This figurative use is quite poetic and common in literature. The key idea is always the same: something opening up widely and deeply.
How It Behaves in a Sentence

As a verb, yawn works in the following ways:

  • She yawned and stretched her arms above her head. (simple past)
  • He is yawning because he stayed up too late. (present continuous)
  • Stop yawning — it's making me yawn too! (gerund/command)
  • The cave yawned open in the side of the mountain. (figurative)
  • I tried not to yawn during the presentation, but I couldn't help it. (suppressing a yawn)

To yawn is to involuntarily open your mouth wide and draw in a deep breath, typically triggered by tiredness, boredom, or the transition between sleep and wakefulness. It is a physical reflex that is social (people notice it), contagious (seeing it makes you do it), and hard to control. Figuratively, the word also describes anything that opens up in a wide, gaping, or vast way. Mastering both the literal and figurative uses will give you full command of this word in any context you encounter it.
17638: "Yawning" as an adjective means wide open, gaping, and vast — especially describing an opening, gap, or empty space that is so large it feels impossible (or very difficult) to cross or fill.

Think about what happens when a person yawns: their mouth opens very wide, creating a deep, open cavity. The adjective borrows exactly that image. When something is described as "yawning," it is open and vast in the same dramatic way — like a mouth wide open in a yawn.

So a yawning chasm is not just a big crack in the ground. It is a crack that is gapingly wide and deep — one that makes you feel small standing at its edge.

"Yawning" doesn't just mean large. It carries a specific sense of:

  • Openness — something gaping, not merely big
  • Depth or emptiness — there is a hollow, vacant quality to it
  • An unbridgeable quality — the gap or opening is so vast that crossing or filling it feels daunting or impossible

This is why "yawning" is almost never used for solid objects (you wouldn't say a "yawning boulder"). It lives in the world of openings, gaps, distances, and differences.
The nouns it almost always lives with

"Yawning" is nearly always placed directly before a noun (this is called attributive use). The most common pairings are:

  • yawning gap — the most common phrase by far
  • yawning chasm — a deep, wide gorge or divide
  • yawning gulf — a vast separation
  • yawning abyss — a bottomless-feeling void
  • yawning void — a huge, empty space
  • yawning divide — a massive difference between two sides
  • yawning hole / yawning cavern — a physical opening

Notice a pattern: all of these words describe openings or separations. That is the natural home of this adjective.

Physical:

  • The explorers peered into a yawning cavern beneath their feet.

(A cave entrance so wide and dark it seemed to swallow everything.)

  • One wrong step and she would fall into the yawning abyss below.

(A terrifyingly wide, deep drop.)

Abstract — differences and divides:

  • There is a yawning gap between what the government promises and what it delivers.

(The difference is enormous and hard to close.)

  • A yawning divide exists between the two communities, built over decades of mistrust.

(A vast, deep separation — not just a disagreement, but something enormous.)

  • The yawning gulf between the wealthy and the poor continues to grow.

(The inequality is vast and widening.)

Emotional or existential:

  • After his retirement, a yawning void opened up in his life.

(A huge, hollow emptiness — not a small gap, but an overwhelming absence.)

"Yawning" (as an adjective) has a slightly formal, literary quality. You will encounter it more often in:

  • Newspaper editorials and serious journalism
  • Books, essays, and academic writing
  • Speeches and formal commentary

In everyday casual conversation, people are more likely to say "a huge gap" or "a massive divide." But "yawning" elevates the description — it makes the vastness feel more vivid and dramatic. When a writer chooses "yawning," they want you to feel how wide and deep the gap is, not just know it intellectually.
An important distinction: what "yawning" does NOT mean

This is where many learners go wrong.

You might think: "Yawning makes people sleepy. So does 'yawning' mean boring or sleep-inducing?"

No. The adjective "yawning" does not mean boring.

The word that means "causing boredom" is soporific or simply boring. "Yawning" the adjective has nothing to do with boredom or tedium. It is purely about vast, open, gaping space or difference.

✅ Correct:

  • a yawning gap in their knowledge
  • a yawning chasm between theory and practice

❌ Incorrect:

  • a yawning speech (meaning boring) — this is wrong
  • a yawning mountain (yawning doesn't describe solid, closed things)

Also note: while you can technically say "the gap was yawning," it sounds unusual. "Yawning" works best — and is almost always used — directly before the noun it describes: a yawning gap, not the gap is yawning.
"Yawning" as an adjective describes something that is wide open, deeply vast, and empty — like a gaping mouth — and is used for gaps, chasms, divides, and voids that feel enormous and hard to bridge.
17639:
A yawp is a loud, harsh, raw cry or shout — one that is unrefined, unpolished, and bursting with energy. It is not the clean, controlled sound of someone calling out calmly. It is the kind of sound that comes from somewhere deep and instinctive, with no attempt to make it pretty or proper.

Think of the sound a crow makes — sharp, grating, forceful. Or the yell someone lets out when they're overwhelmed with emotion and simply cannot hold it in anymore. That rough, almost wild quality is the heart of a yawp.
What makes a yawp different from a regular cry or shout?

Words like cry, shout, scream, and yell describe loud sounds, but they are fairly neutral. A yawp carries something extra: it is unrestrained and untamed. It does not care about sounding dignified. There is a roughness to it, even a crudeness. You wouldn't describe a trained singer hitting a high note as a yawp. But you might describe a street vendor hollering in a crowded market, a bird shrieking over a rooftop, or a person letting out a guttural battle cry as a yawp.

In short: a yawp is loud + harsh + raw + free of any self-consciousness.
Who or what can produce a yawp?

• Animals: The word suits harsh animal sounds — a dog's sharp yelp, a crow's cawing, a parrot's squawk. Anything loud and unmusical.
  • Humans: A person can let out a yawp — particularly when they are overwhelmed by emotion (joy, pain, anger, excitement) and express it loudly without filtering themselves.
  • Metaphorically: Ideas, voices, or forces can "yawp" when they burst out boldly and unapologetically into the world.

This is where the word becomes truly powerful. A yawp is not just noise — it can represent a bold declaration of existence. The idea of saying, loudly and without shame: I am here. I am alive. I exist.

This meaning became deeply attached to the word because of the American poet Walt Whitman, who wrote one of the most famous lines in all of English poetry:

"I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world."

In this line, Whitman is not just describing a sound. He is saying: I will express myself fully, wildly, without apology — even if the world finds it uncivilized ("barbaric"). His yawp is a declaration of his full, unfiltered self sent out into the world.

Because of Whitman, the word carries this extra layer: a yawp can mean any raw, fearless, full-throated expression of one's inner self — an act of refusing to be quiet or subdued.
The secondary meaning: noisy, empty talk

Less commonly, yawp can also refer to loud, foolish chatter — the kind of noise someone makes when they're talking a lot but saying very little of value. This usage treats a yawp as something more annoying than inspiring: like a person who brags and blusters without substance. This meaning is much rarer and older, and when you encounter the word today, it almost always carries the more powerful, Whitman-influenced meaning.
The overall feeling the word conveys

When a writer uses the word "yawp," they are almost always trying to communicate:

  • Rawness — something unpolished, not cleaned up for public consumption
  • Vitality — full of life-force, not weak or timid
  • Freedom — uncaged, not holding back
  • Authenticity — however rough it sounds, it is real

It is a word with personality. It sounds like what it means — even the word itself has a blunt, slightly rough quality.

A yawp is a loud, harsh, unrefined cry or shout — one that is raw, uninhibited, and full of energy. At its most meaningful, it stands for the bold, unashamed expression of one's full self, sent out into the world without apology. It is the sound of something — or someone — refusing to be silenced.
